Messages.Author: Brian
Messages.Body:
From the V:EKN official tournament rules:

2.4 Spectator Responsibilities
Spectators are expected to remain silent during the course of a game
and are not allowed to communicate with players in any way while a
game is in progress. Spectators who believe they have observed rules
violations should inform a judge, but they must not interfere with the
game. Players have the right to request that any person, other than
tournament officials, not observe their game. All such requests must
be made through a judge.

Two weeks ago, I was ousted in a finals game, which I went into in
second place. Since I was ousted first, and my predator went into the
game in first place, I knew that I wanted him to sweep the table, so
that I could get second. Was it my duty to step aside once ousted,
turning me into a spectator? Or did I still have the right to speak
to the players, since convincing my predator not to table-split could
have gotten me second place instead of third? At first I was OK with
"you're ousted, you're done playing, so you're done talking", but then
later at home I realized that I still had something at stake and still
had the ability to do something about it, which by game theory makes
me a "bona fide player".

So, which is it? How am I treated when I'm ousted, but still have
something on the line? Can I tell my old predator that I think he can
take the last two on his own (boy I hope), or may I be asked to not
observe "their" (my) game?

-- Brian

I've always gone by: Once you're ousted, you're a specter. Trotting
out the argument about having something at stake could apply to other
situations, such as a player on the bubble for making it into the finals
watching a game in the last round where one of the players might leapfrog
him. He would therefore likewise have something at stake in terms of the
tournament, but this doesn't give him the right to interfere with the
game.

Fred

I would go with this as well. When I run a tourney, the "places" go
as follows

VPs in Final
If tie on VPs for first, then previous results.
All on 0VPs, order of ousting.

That way, no people in the final who are ousted quickly have
any real reason to want to influence the game. I don't know whether
this is really right or wrong, but as I don't usually have graded
prizes for position, that doesn't tend to make for much deal anyway.

Just my way of doing things.

Assuming the judge has no discretion about it, that would be kind of
ridiculous. Legally, a player could ask always for his property back
at any time, regardless of tournament rules of course - as long as
he didn't care what tournament penalties he was assessed.

But I would think the rules would be better written to waive this particular
option for players who were ousted. Presumably, a judge can always ask a
spectator (including ousted players) to vacate if they became a problem in
his eyes.

Fred

> the current game) is an in-game concern.

The rules as written seem pretty clear in saying that coaching,
once you're no longer part of the game, isn't allowable for
"former players" any more than for "spectators".

It might be possible to rewrite the rules as you suggest,
drawing a distinction between "ex-players" and "spectators",
but I'm not sure it would be a good thing. Since you have
nothing but advice that you can offer people still in the game,
once ousted, it seems to me that you'd pretty much just be
coaching (or manipulating), and in the interests of time and
fairness that should probably be prohibited for ex-players as
much as for spectators.

On the other parts of the rule, as I read it, this:

"Players have the right to request that any person, other than
tournament officials, not observe their game. All such requests
must be made through a judge."

doesn't necessarily imply that all such requests must be
granted, ie it may be up to the judge whether or not any
particular request is a reasonable one, and what action to
take in response to it.

This part:

"Spectators are expected to remain silent during the course of

a game and are not permitted to communicate with players in

any way while a game is in progress."

I'm not so sure about. I think it's definitely proper to
disallow communicating with players, but total silence is more
than is generally (I think) asked of spectators of games. I
see no problem, generally, with spectators talking among
themselves. There is the issue that the players might then
overhear something they shouldn't, but not all situations are
vulnerable to that problem. (If there's a glass wall between
the spectators and the players, for example.)

Josh

Well.

Technically, if I'm reading the rules right, you shouldn't even
tell them to stop if you think you saw a rules violation. You
should just silently go and find the judge and tell him or her.
He or she would then go over to the table and investigate, and
presumably correct the error if possible.

As you say, this is a rather cumbersome process for "minor"
errors of the sort that are often made many times in a single
game (in my experience). But it's the only one that's described
in the tournament rules.

I'm not sure just now what ought to be done about that, but my
instinct is that just not enforcing the "all rules corrections
through a judge" rule isn't the best answer. :-)

Josh

remain seated in spite of having been ousted. This is fine if he just
sits there, but usually he issues some remark, sometimes related to
the game, sometimes not, but always intruding upon the game - which

player to leave is unfair because it may remove some of the enjoyment

>

It never fails to amuse me how inappropriately the word "fascist"
is often used. Esp. when someone wants to demonize something.

Personally, I subscribe to there being no such thing as "harmless
interference." There was an individual at Origins, whom I shall
decline to name, that kept forcefully pointing out errors that
players were making, rather than quietly mentioning them to
the judge. Because he was being such a distraction, people were
unable to concentrate and were unable to correct their mistakes
themselves and were prone to making even more errors. This
happened in spite of the judge telling him that if he wanted to
watch, he had to keep quiet. Naturally, my lack of tolerance
and my participation in the game prompted me to angrily chase
him off when he was apparently, physically unable to restrain
himself.

My point is that kibitzing is often irritating and distracting to
people that are attempting to concentrate on the strategic
game at hand. If you are not playing in the game, you shouldn't
be bothering those who are. It's not being fascist, it's enforcing
the rules of most card games. Don't believe me? Go try kibitzing
in a poker game for money or a euchre game in Michigan or
Canada. If you come out unscathed, it's likely because you can
run really fast.

Obviously, all of this does not apply to more casual environments.
While tournaments can be casual, it's not fair to expect them to
be.

Regards,
Noal

It's not clearly spelled out, no.

It's probably assumed by the current rules to be implicit in
the common usage of "player" and "spectator". That is, a
"player" is "one that plays" as in "a person who plays a game";
by "plays" meaning "to engage or take part in a game".

So, someone whose participation in the game has ended is
assumed to no longer be a player in this sense.

9.1 refers to them as a player, yes, and they *were* "one of
the players in that game", but that's more of a past-tense
sense than an ongoing thing, as I read it. That is, I think
what 9.1 is saying is, all those people *were* players in
that game; it's not saying that they *remain* players in that
game after they've been ousted - by usual definitions of
"player" it seems to me nonsensical to consider them to still
be "playing" the game after they've explicitly already been
removed from the game.

There has not been, as far as I know, any ruling to this
effect (ie explicitly stating that ex-players are now
spectators) but it seems to me like it's pretty obviously
the intent of the rules. Regardless, they could certainly be
clarified on this point, and maybe they will be.

>

Nor does it need to be. If being a player requires not having been
ousted, then someone who is ousted is not a player. There can be no
"player, even an ousted one" any more than there can be a "reader,
even an illiterate one". We need not know exactly what makes a player
for the purposes of this argument; just that you can be ousted and
remain one is sufficient.

On the contrary, LSJ has previously stated that the rulebook is not to
be taken as seriously as other more formal documents, as its main
purpose is teaching new players the game as opposed to chiseling out
the finer points of the rules (like definitions of "player" and
"spectator", I assume).

I shall have to look up this "coaching" thing. Right now I think
they're talking about when a player makes all of his or her
non-obvious decisions based on what another person tells them to. I
doubt table talk about strategy is considered "coaching" because it is
abstract, not concrete.

"Oust that guy if you can" = table talk
"Play the Dreams of the Sphinx to contest, bleed with Ozmo with a
Govern and Bonding if he blocks" = coaching

I do not see the harm in a player coaching another player, only when a
spectator plays for someone do I see a problem, because telling
another player what to do exactly could be part of a trade.

> It's probably assumed by the current rules to be implicit in
> the common usage of "player" and "spectator". That is, a
> "player" is "one that plays" as in "a person who plays a game";
> by "plays" meaning "to engage or take part in a game".
>
> So, someone whose participation in the game has ended is
> assumed to no longer be a player in this sense.

If one's behavior affects the game, and he stands to gain a table win
or some tournament points from it, then his participation has not
ended.

A Methuselah can get tournament points and even a game win after they
are ousted because the assignment of these can change through
subsequent play. And even when they cannot play cards or effects,
table talk is not illegal for normal players and might indeed improve
their position. Thus, with both stakes in the game (directly) and a
way to influence the outcome of the game (table talk), they are a
player, even by your definition above (someone whose participation has
not ended).

Contrast with a spectator, who is unable to get VPs, tournament
points, or a table win from such interference. They have no direct
stakes in the game and should remain uninvolved.

(Betting on the outcome of a game = indirect stakes)
(Winning or losing in the game = direct stakes)

It seems reasonable that a Methuselah who is ousted should be reduced
to vying for "tournament points". This reduces them to an extremely
minor participant in the game, without pretending that it doesn't
concern or involve them.

> 9.1 refers to them as a player, yes, and they *were* "one of
> the players in that game", but that's more of a past-tense
> sense than an ongoing thing, as I read it.

Section 9.1 said "the winner is the player with...", and "is" is
present tense. Although you spoke in the past tense, the rules (to my
knowledge) do not.

> it's not saying that they *remain* players in that
> game after they've been ousted -

I disagree. It is implicitly saying such.

> by usual definitions of
> "player" it seems to me nonsensical to consider them to still
> be "playing" the game after they've explicitly already been
> removed from the game.

It could also be considered nonsensical that someone who is removed
from the game can still win. Jyhad is not like most games in this
respect, and it appears Jyhad's definition of "player" is tailored to
fit that.

How "removed from the game" is someone if they are still in the
running for winning?
-- Brian

Messages.Author: Brian
Messages.Body:
> I've always gone by: Once you're ousted, you're a specter. Trotting

> out the argument about having something at stake could apply to other
> situations, such as a player on the bubble for making it into the finals
> watching a game in the last round where one of the players might leapfrog
> him. He would therefore likewise have something at stake in terms of the
> tournament, but this doesn't give him the right to interfere with the
> game.

In someone else's game, you may have something at stake, but not
DIRECTLY. Directly, in this case, meaning having to do with the ways
victory is measured in the game.

Table Win at stake = directly at stake.
Placed a bet (which is illegal anyway)= indirectly at stake.
Tournament Points at stake = directly at stake.
Want John, and not Mark, in the finals = indirectly at stake.

Having Mark in the finals may harm you much more than getting a few
extra table points, but that is immaterial to the matter at hand and
cannot be directly measured. You should be able to put in in your own
game, where tournament points and maybe the table win are up for
grabs, but not in John and Mark's game. You are not a player in that
game.

The situation you suggested (ousted player speaking freely to members
of another table) certainly makes me sound ridiculous, but is not my
argument. I challenge you to show me how anything bad could come
about from allowing a person to continue to speak when ousted. They
may talk without much ground to stand on, but then, players around
here do that anyway. :)

-- Brian
